indiaMissions.title: Bakht Singh and the indigenous assemblies
indiaMissions.region: Punjab and Sindh (1930s), Tamil Nadu (Madras), Andhra Pradesh and Telangana (Hyderabad), with assemblies across India and in the diaspora
indiaMissions.summary: Bakht Singh Chabra (1903–2000), a Punjabi Sikh who became a Christian while studying in Canada, was independent India’s best-known evangelist and the founder of a network of self-governing, self-supporting “assemblies” — beginning with Jehovah Shammah in Madras (1941) and centred from the 1950s on Hebron in Hyderabad — that rejected denominational structures, foreign money and Western church forms in favour of what he took to be the New Testament pattern.
indiaMissions.story:
Bakht Singh was born on 6 June 1903 at Joiya in Sargodha district of the Punjab (now in Pakistan) into a prosperous Sikh family. Educated partly in mission-run schools, he was by his own account hostile to Christianity as a young man and once tore up a copy of the Bible. In 1926 he went to England to study engineering and in 1928–29 moved to Canada, where friendships with evangelical families and his own reading of the New Testament led to the conversion he dated to 1929; he was baptised as a believer in February 1932. When he returned to India in 1933 his family disowned him, and he began an itinerant, unsalaried preaching ministry.

Through the mid-1930s he preached in the Punjab, Sindh (notably Karachi) and the North-West, and from 1937–38 he was invited by Anglican, Methodist and other missions to hold campaigns in South India. His meetings in Madras and elsewhere in the Tamil and Telugu country drew large crowds, many of them nominal members of established Protestant churches, and were widely described as a revival marked by public confession, restitution and Bible study. Tension soon followed: Bakht Singh insisted that those converted should be baptised by immersion and gather as a New Testament fellowship, and mission churches accused him of drawing members away. In 1941 the first assembly, Jehovah Shammah, was formed in Madras, and its annual “Holy Convocation” became a defining feature of the movement.

The assemblies followed a deliberately simple order drawn from his reading of Acts and the Epistles and resembling Brethren ecclesiology: no denominational name, no ordained clergy or titles, plural elders and recognised “workers”, weekly breaking of bread, believers’ baptism, worship seated on the floor with Indian lyrics and psalm-singing, men and women seated separately with women’s heads covered, open-air processions, and long sessions of Bible exposition. Financially the movement refused public appeals and foreign subsidies; workers lived “by faith” on gifts from Indian believers, and hospitality and common meals were central. His ecclesiology paralleled that of Watchman Nee’s “Little Flock” in China, whose writings circulated among Indian assemblies, and echoed the faith principles of the Brethren missionary Anthony Norris Groves in the Godavari delta a century earlier.

In 1950 Bakht Singh moved his base to Hyderabad, where the Hebron compound at Golconda Cross Roads became the headquarters, publishing centre and venue for convocations that drew tens of thousands of people each year. Assemblies multiplied especially in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, but also in Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra, the Punjab and the north, and among Indian migrants in Britain, North America and the Gulf. He travelled abroad repeatedly from the 1940s onwards and was received by Western evangelicals as a model of an indigenous church leader, while himself insisting on Indian control and self-support.

After strokes in the 1990s left him incapacitated, he died in Hyderabad on 17 September 2000. Because the assemblies had no written constitution or central denomination, their unity after his death depended on personal ties among elders and workers, and observers note local fragmentation and leadership disputes. Supporters have claimed figures ranging from several thousand to over ten thousand assemblies and fellowships in India and abroad; these totals have not been independently verified and probably include loosely affiliated groups.

Historians such as Robert Frykenberg and Roger Hedlund treat Bakht Singh as a pioneer of the Indian-led, mission-independent churches that became a major strand of Indian Christianity after independence. His critics, including leaders of the mainline churches, regarded the movement as separatist and accused it of “sheep-stealing”; others note its strictly patriarchal ordering of worship and the heavy weight placed on one charismatic founder. Its lasting significance lies in demonstrating, within a generation of the end of colonial rule, that a large Protestant movement could be led, financed and shaped entirely by Indians.

indiaMissions.title: Church unions: Church of South India (1947) and Church of North India (1970)
indiaMissions.region: South India (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana; Jaffna in Sri Lanka) and North India from the Punjab to the Northeast
indiaMissions.summary: Indian Christians, frustrated by the imported denominational divisions of the missionary era, pioneered the most ambitious church unions of the twentieth century: the Church of South India (27 September 1947), the first union anywhere of episcopal and non-episcopal churches, and the Church of North India (29 November 1970), which joined Anglicans, Presbyterians, Congregationalists, Baptists, Methodists, Brethren and Disciples.
indiaMissions.story:
By 1900 Protestant Christianity in India was divided into dozens of mission-derived denominations, often separated by comity agreements that assigned districts to particular societies. Indian Christians increasingly argued that these divisions were foreign imports irrelevant to their situation. The first fruits were unions among similar churches: the South India United Church (1908) brought together congregations founded by Scottish and American Presbyterians and Reformed (including the Arcot Mission) with Congregationalists of the London Missionary Society and the American Madura Mission, and the United Church of Northern India (1924) did the same for Presbyterians and Congregationalists in the north. The National Missionary Council (1914), which became the National Christian Council in 1923, and the influence of the Edinburgh conference of 1910 gave the movement an institutional home.

The decisive step came at Tranquebar in May 1919, when thirty-three ministers, almost all Indian, from the Anglican Church and the South India United Church met and declared that union was the remedy for the weakness of the Indian church. Taking the Lambeth Quadrilateral as a basis — the Scriptures, the creeds, the two dominical sacraments and the historic episcopate — they opened negotiations that drew in the Anglican dioceses of Madras, Tinnevelly, Travancore and Cochin, and Dornakal, the South India United Church and, from 1925, the Methodist Church of South India. V. S. Azariah, the first Indian Anglican bishop, was a leading advocate. The hardest question was ministry: how could ministers without episcopal ordination serve alongside bishops in a church that accepted the historic episcopate?

The Scheme of Union, published in 1929 and repeatedly revised, answered with a compromise. All existing ministers of the uniting churches were accepted as ministers of the united church without re-ordination; all future ordinations would be by bishops; and for an interim period of thirty years no congregation would be forced to accept a minister whose ordination it could not in conscience receive. The union was inaugurated on 27 September 1947 in St George’s Cathedral, Madras, six weeks after independence. The Church of South India began with about one million members in fourteen dioceses; Michael Hollis became the first moderator and Lesslie Newbigin, consecrated bishop of Madura and Ramnad, became its best-known theological interpreter.

The union was controversial abroad. The Lambeth Conference of 1948 was divided, Anglo-Catholics objected to the acceptance of non-episcopally ordained ministers, and some congregations formerly of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in the Nandyal area of Andhra stayed out, remaining Anglican until they joined the Church of North India in 1970. Full communion with the Church of England and other Anglican provinces came only gradually. Negotiations with the Lutheran churches of South India produced agreed theological statements but no union, and Baptists, most Pentecostals and the Syrian churches remained outside.

In the north, a round-table conference at Lucknow in 1929 began talks that produced a Plan of Union, issued in successive editions to 1965. Learning from the South Indian debates, the northern churches unified their ministries from the outset through a service of reconciliation in which existing ministers received a mutual laying on of hands, avoiding an interim period. The Church of North India was inaugurated on 29 November 1970 at All Saints’ Cathedral, Nagpur, uniting the Church of India (Anglican), the United Church of Northern India, the Council of Baptist Churches in Northern India, the Church of the Brethren in India, the Disciples of Christ and the British and Australasian Methodist conferences. The American-related Methodist Church in Southern Asia voted at the last stage not to join and later became the autonomous Methodist Church in India (1981). The Church of Pakistan was formed on a similar basis in the same month.

In 1978 the Church of South India, the Church of North India and the Mar Thoma Syrian Church formed the Communion of Churches in India, recognising each other’s ministries and sacraments. Both united churches are members of the World Council of Churches and of the Anglican Communion, as well as the World Communion of Reformed Churches and the Council for World Mission. Their later history has been less heroic than their founding: Dalits form the majority of their members but have struggled for fair representation; diocesan elections have been fought along caste and regional lines; and both churches have faced extensive litigation over elections and the sale or misuse of large colonial-era property holdings. In the 2020s the Church of South India was troubled by court challenges to its 2022 constitutional amendments and the moderator’s election, and by an Enforcement Directorate investigation (2022) into alleged capitation fees at its medical college at Karakonam in Kerala.

indiaMissions.title: Modern Catholic mission: Mother Teresa, education, ashrams and inculturation
indiaMissions.region: All India: West Bengal (Kolkata), Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, the Northeast
indiaMissions.summary: After independence the Catholic Church — India’s largest Christian body, spanning the Latin, Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara churches — Indianised its hierarchy, sent Kerala priests and sisters across the country, ran a vast network of schools and hospitals, produced Mother Teresa’s Missionaries of Charity, and experimented boldly with Hindu-inspired ashrams and liturgy, while facing criticism, caste conflict and scandal.
indiaMissions.story:
At independence the Catholic Church was already the largest Christian community in India, heir to the Thomas Christians of Kerala, the Portuguese Padroado, the Jesuit missions and nineteenth-century missions such as the Belgian Jesuits in Chota Nagpur. The Catholic Bishops’ Conference of India was founded in 1944, Valerian Gracias of Bombay became the first Indian cardinal in 1953, and foreign bishops were steadily replaced by Indians. As the government restricted visas for new foreign missionaries from the 1950s, the church came to rely on its own clergy and religious, above all from Kerala: Syro-Malabar and Latin Catholic priests and sisters from Kerala staffed schools, hospitals and parishes from Punjab to Arunachal, and Rome erected Syro-Malabar “mission eparchies” in central and northern India from the 1960s (Chanda, Sagar, Satna, Ujjain, Bijnor, Jagdalpur, Gorakhpur, Rajkot and others).

The best-known figure of this era was Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu, an ethnic Albanian from Skopje who arrived in India as a Loreto sister in 1929 and taught at St Mary’s School, Entally, in Calcutta. On 10 September 1946, on a train to Darjeeling, she experienced what she called a “call within a call” to serve the poorest. Leaving Loreto in 1948 and wearing a white sari with a blue border, she began work in the slums; the Missionaries of Charity were approved as a diocesan congregation on 7 October 1950. Nirmal Hriday, a home for the dying in a former pilgrims’ rest-house beside the Kali temple at Kalighat, opened in 1952, followed by Shishu Bhavan for abandoned children (1955) and leprosy work culminating in Shanti Nagar near Asansol. She received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and the Bharat Ratna in 1980; at her death on 5 September 1997 the congregation had around four thousand sisters in 123 countries. She was given a state funeral, beatified in 2003 and canonised on 4 September 2016. Letters published in 2007 revealed decades of spiritual darkness and sense of God’s absence.

Mother Teresa was also the subject of sustained criticism. Christopher Hitchens (The Missionary Position, 1995), the Calcutta-born physician Aroup Chatterjee and a 2013 study by Serge Larivée and colleagues at the Université de Montréal questioned the standard of medical care in her homes (limited pain relief, reuse of needles, little diagnosis), her acceptance of donations from figures such as Charles Keating and the Duvalier family, the opacity of the order’s finances, and her uncompromising opposition to abortion and contraception. Hindu nationalist leaders, notably RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat in 2015, alleged that conversion was the motive of her service, which the order denied. In 2018 a sister and an employee of a Missionaries of Charity home in Ranchi were arrested over the alleged sale of infants, prompting government inspections of the order’s child-care homes; and in December 2021 the government refused to renew the order’s licence to receive foreign funds, restoring it in January 2022 after public protest.

A quite different strand of Catholic mission sought to meet Hinduism at its contemplative heart. In 1950 the French priest Jules Monchanin and the Breton Benedictine Henri Le Saux, who took the name Swami Abhishiktananda, founded Saccidananda Ashram (Shantivanam) on the Kaveri near Kulithalai in Tamil Nadu, adopting saffron robes, vegetarian diet and Sanskrit terminology. The English Benedictine Bede Griffiths, who co-founded Kurisumala Ashram in the Kerala hills in 1958 with the Belgian Cistercian Francis Mahieu in the Syro-Malankara rite, led Shantivanam from 1968 until his death in 1993 and made it an international centre of Hindu–Christian dialogue. After the Second Vatican Council, D. S. Amalorpavadass’s National Biblical, Catechetical and Liturgical Centre in Bangalore (1967) promoted an Indian rite; Rome approved twelve points of liturgical adaptation in 1969 — sitting on the floor, the arati of lights, Indian gestures — but halted a proposed Indian anaphora in the 1970s. Theologians such as Raimon Panikkar (The Unknown Christ of Hinduism, 1964), the Jesuits Jacques Dupuis and Michael Amaladoss and the spiritual writer Anthony de Mello made India a centre of the theology of religions, and both Dupuis and de Mello later received notifications from the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith.

Catholic institutions became one of the most visible Christian contributions to Indian life: schools and colleges such as St Xavier’s in Calcutta and Bombay and Loyola College, Madras (1925), the Catholic Health Association of India (1943), St John’s Medical College, Bangalore (1963), and the relief agency Caritas India (1962). Among the Adivasi peoples of Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Odisha, where Belgian Jesuits had worked since the 1880s, the church grew into a tribal-majority community; Telesphore Toppo of Ranchi became the first Adivasi cardinal in 2003. Social-action Jesuits founded the Indian Social Institute (1951), and the Jesuit Stan Swamy, who worked for Adivasi land rights in Jharkhand, was arrested in 2020 in the Bhima Koregaon case under anti-terror law and died in custody in July 2021, aged 84. Sister Rani Maria Vattalil, a Kerala nun working among the poor near Indore, was murdered in 1995 by a man hired by local money-lenders; her killer later sought forgiveness from her family, and she was beatified in 2017. Paul VI’s visit to the International Eucharistic Congress in Bombay in 1964 was the first papal journey to India, and John Paul II, visiting in 1986 and 1999, signed the post-synodal exhortation Ecclesia in Asia in New Delhi.

The modern Catholic story also includes deep internal tensions. Dalits form the majority of Catholics in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh, yet separate seating, cemeteries and festival processions persisted in some parishes, leading to clashes such as those at Eraiyur in Villupuram district in 2008; in 2016 the bishops’ conference published a Policy of Dalit Empowerment that acknowledged caste discrimination within the church. In Kerala, a disputed land sale in the Syro-Malabar archdiocese of Ernakulam-Angamaly (2016–18) and a bitter dispute over the mode of celebrating the Holy Mass from 2021 divided clergy and laity, while the trial of Bishop Franco Mulakkal on charges of raping a nun ended in his acquittal by a Kottayam court in January 2022, a verdict that the complainant’s supporters contested.

indiaMissions.summary: As foreign missionaries were squeezed out after 1947, Indian evangelicals created their own cross-cultural missions — the Friends Missionary Prayer Band (from 1959), the Indian Evangelical Mission (1965), Indian branches of Operation Mobilisation (from 1963–64) and Campus Crusade, and later hundreds of agencies grouped in the India Missions Association (1977) — sending southern and northeastern Christians to plant churches among unreached peoples of north and central India, with notable growth but also controversy over money, methods and conversion.
indiaMissions.story:
Independence changed the conditions of mission. The Niyogi Committee report of 1956 in Madhya Pradesh called for curbs on foreign missionaries, and from the 1960s the central government sharply limited new missionary visas. Western missionary numbers fell steadily, and Indian churches — whose own earlier initiatives included the Indian Missionary Society (1903) and the National Missionary Society (1905) — took up the task. A new evangelical infrastructure emerged: the Evangelical Fellowship of India (1951), the Union of Evangelical Students of India (1954), the Hindustan Bible Institute founded in Madras by Paul Gupta (1952) and Union Biblical Seminary at Yavatmal (1953, moved to Pune in 1983).

The Friends Missionary Prayer Band grew out of a prayer circle of young Tamil Christians who met in December 1959 at Kovilpatti and nearby Pannaivilai in Tirunelveli district, among them Theodore Williams, Emil Jebasingh and Patrick Joshua. Its model was distinctive: thousands of small “prayer bands” in Tamil churches gave monthly sums to support Tamil missionaries working in other language areas. Five pioneers began work among the Malayali hill people at Periyamalai in Dharmapuri district in June 1967, and from the 1970s FMPB concentrated on north India, adopting districts and peoples in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Gujarat and the Himalaya. The Indian Evangelical Mission was launched by Indian members of the Evangelical Fellowship of India meeting at Devlali, Maharashtra, on 15 January 1965, with Theodore Williams as its long-serving leader; it sent Indian workers to tribal areas of central India, the Andamans and beyond, and stressed Indian funding and accountability.

Operation Mobilisation brought a different energy. In 1963–64 George Verwer’s teams drove trucks overland from Europe to India, distributing literature and recruiting young Indians for summer and year-long teams; OM India soon became one of the largest employers of Indian Christian volunteers and later, under Joseph D’Souza, combined evangelism with Dalit rights advocacy and a network of Good Shepherd English-medium schools for Dalit children. Campus Crusade for Christ (from 1968) distributed the JESUS film in dozens of Indian languages, and Youth With A Mission, the Bible League, Scripture Union and many others established Indian branches. The churches of Mizoram and Nagaland, themselves products of earlier missions, created their own mission boards in the 1960s and 1970s and sent hundreds of workers to other states and abroad. The India Missions Association, founded in 1977, became the umbrella body for hundreds of Indian agencies.

The Lausanne Congress (1974), the church growth school of Donald McGavran (who had himself worked in central India) and the AD2000 and Joshua Project initiatives of the 1990s focused attention on “unreached people groups”, and north India’s Hindi belt was described as the most populous unevangelised region in the world. Indian agencies divided the region by district and people group, set up hostels, literacy classes, clinics and tailoring centres, trained local believers as evangelists, and planted small congregations, often house churches. In the 1990s reports of a large church-planting movement among Bhojpuri-speaking Dalits and backward castes in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, popularised by David Garrison and Victor Choudhrie, attracted global attention, though their scale has been hard to verify. Pentecostal and charismatic healing ministries, from D. G. S. Dhinakaran’s Jesus Calls (1970s) to the independent prayer centres of the Punjab in the 2010s, grew alongside the agencies and often outpaced them.

The largest and most controversial agency was Gospel for Asia, founded in Texas in 1979 by the Kerala-born K. P. Yohannan, which raised large sums from Western donors to support “native missionaries” and built the Believers Church (1993), an episcopal church based at Thiruvalla in Kerala that was renamed Believers Eastern Church in 2017. In 2015 the Evangelical Council for Financial Accountability in the United States expelled GFA for violating its standards, and in 2019 GFA settled a US class action alleging misuse of donations for 37 million dollars without admitting wrongdoing. In India, income-tax authorities searched Believers Church premises in 2020 over alleged diversion of foreign contributions. Yohannan died in May 2024 after being struck by a car in Texas.

By the early twenty-first century India had become one of the major missionary-sending countries of the majority world, almost entirely through internal cross-cultural mission. The results were uneven but real: new congregations among tribal peoples of central India, Dalit communities in the north, and in the Punjab a rapid growth of independent Pentecostal churches. The work also generated serious tensions: accusations of inducement and “fraudulent” conversion underpinned anti-conversion laws; dependence on foreign funds made agencies vulnerable when the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act was tightened in 2010 and 2020 (Compassion International ended its Indian operations in 2017); southern missionaries were sometimes paternalistic toward northern and tribal cultures; competition between agencies and inflated reporting of converts and churches distorted the picture; and missionaries and converts faced social boycott and violence.

indiaMissions.title: Bible translation and print in Indian languages
indiaMissions.region: All India: Tranquebar and Madras (Tamil), Serampore and Calcutta (Bengali and many northern languages), Kottayam (Malayalam), Mangalore (Kannada, Tulu), Khasi and Mizo hills, Bangalore (Bible Society of India)
indiaMissions.summary: From Ziegenbalg’s Tamil New Testament printed at Tranquebar in 1714–15 and the Serampore press’s translations into some forty languages, to the Bible Society of India’s 2023 count of complete Bibles in 91 Indian languages and New Testaments in 86 more, Bible translation has been one of the most far-reaching Christian activities in India — shaping modern prose, typography, grammars and dictionaries, while raising enduring questions about vocabulary, caste and cultural authority.
indiaMissions.story:
The St Thomas Christians of Kerala used the Syriac Bible and liturgy for over a millennium without producing a Malayalam Bible, and the Portuguese Catholic missions concentrated on catechisms, confessional manuals and lives of Christ rather than vernacular Scripture: the Jesuit Henrique Henriques’s Tamil Doctrina Christam (1578) was among the first books printed in an Indian script, and Thomas Stephens’s Kristapurana (1616) retold the Bible in Marathi-Konkani verse. Protestant translation began with Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg at the Danish colony of Tranquebar. Working with Tamil scholars, he translated the New Testament, which was printed on the mission press with Tamil type cast in Halle and appeared in 1714–15 — the first printed Bible translation in any Indian language. Benjamin Schultze completed the Old Testament by 1728 and also worked on Telugu and Hindustani, and Johann Philipp Fabricius’s revision, admired for its idiomatic Tamil, remained in use for over a century.

The Serampore Mission (from 1800) turned translation into an industry. William Carey, with pandits such as Mrityunjay Vidyalankar and Indian typecutters led by Panchanan Karmakar and his apprentice Manohar, issued the Bengali New Testament in 1801 and went on to translate or supervise translations into Sanskrit, Marathi, Hindi, Oriya, Punjabi, Assamese and many other languages and dialects. Despite a fire in March 1812 that destroyed type, paper and manuscripts, by Carey’s death in 1834 the Serampore press had issued complete Bibles in six languages and New Testaments or portions in some thirty more. Many were hurried and later replaced, but they established fonts, spelling conventions and a demand for vernacular print. Henry Martyn, an East India Company chaplain, translated the New Testament into Hindustani (Urdu; printed 1814) and Persian; Benjamin Bailey of the Church Missionary Society at Kottayam, who cut his own Malayalam types, completed the Malayalam Bible in 1841; the Basel Mission at Mangalore worked in Kannada and Tulu; and American missionaries produced Marathi, Tamil and Telugu versions.

From 1811 auxiliaries of the British and Foreign Bible Society in Calcutta, Bombay, Madras and North India coordinated revision committees and printing. Revisions such as the Tamil Union Version of 1871, the Telugu and Kannada versions of the late nineteenth century and the Hindi version of the early twentieth century became the standard “old versions” still loved in many churches. Indian translators grew in prominence: Pandita Ramabai learned Hebrew and Greek and translated the whole Bible into simple Marathi at Mukti, completing it shortly before her death in 1922. In the Northeast, Welsh Calvinistic Methodists created the written Khasi language from 1841 and completed the Khasi Bible in 1891, and the Mizo Bible was completed in 1959; for many hill peoples the Bible was the first book in their language. The Bible Society auxiliaries became autonomous in the 1940s and took their present form as the Bible Society of India, headquartered in Bangalore, in 1956.

After the Second Vatican Council Catholics, who had earlier relied on Latin-based or devotional translations, produced new vernacular Bibles such as the Malayalam POC Bible (1981), and joint Catholic–Protestant versions such as the Tamil Thiruviviliam (1995). Dynamic-equivalence “common language” translations, the Easy-to-Read Version, Wycliffe- and SIL-related projects, the Indian Institute for Cross-Cultural Communication and, from 2017–19, the openly licensed Indian Revised Version produced by Indian teams expanded scripture into tribal and minority languages and digital, audio and Braille formats.

The Bible Society of India’s 2023 status report counted complete Bibles in 91 Indian languages (84 Protestant and 7 interconfessional), New Testaments in 86 further languages, audio Bibles in 69 and Braille Bibles in 15, with about 110 translation projects under way. Yet the 2011 census recorded 121 languages with at least 10,000 speakers and Ethnologue lists over 400 living languages in India, so many communities still lack scripture; the Bible Society estimates that at least 300 languages need translation work.

Translation’s cultural impact was profound and contested. Missionary and Indian Christian scholarship produced foundational grammars and dictionaries — Robert Caldwell’s Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian Languages (1856), Hermann Gundert’s Malayalam–English dictionary (1872) and Ferdinand Kittel’s Kannada–English dictionary (1894) — and helped standardise modern prose in Bengali, Malayalam, Tamil and many northeastern languages. Lamin Sanneh and others argue that translation, by valuing the vernacular, unintentionally empowered local cultures and nationalisms. Critics point to stilted early versions, the choice of Sanskritised or Persianised vocabulary that sometimes alienated Dalit and tribal readers, the deepening of the Hindi–Urdu divide through separate Christian versions, the long separation of Catholic and Protestant translations, and the use of scripture distribution in campaigns that opponents of conversion regard as aggressive.

indiaMissions.title: Education, print, social reform and the debates over conversion
indiaMissions.region: All India, especially Bengal, Madras Presidency, Bombay, Kerala, the Punjab and the Northeast
indiaMissions.summary: Christian missions built many of India’s first modern colleges, women’s schools, presses and hospitals, campaigned on sati, caste disabilities and women’s education, and provoked Hindu, Muslim and Sikh reform movements — while their social role has been fiercely debated, from Gandhi’s rejection of proselytism and Ambedkar’s critique of caste in the churches to the Niyogi report, the Constituent Assembly’s right to “propagate” and today’s polemics over conversion.
indiaMissions.story:
Education was the most visible missionary contribution to modern India. From the charity schools of Tranquebar to Serampore College (1818, empowered by a Danish charter of 1827 to grant degrees), Alexander Duff’s General Assembly’s Institution in Calcutta (1830, now Scottish Church College), Wilson College in Bombay (1832), the Madras Christian College (school 1837, college from the 1860s), St John’s College, Agra (1850), Forman Christian College, Lahore (1864) and St Stephen’s College, Delhi (1881), Christian institutions trained much of the English-educated elite. Government grants-in-aid after Wood’s Despatch of 1854 multiplied mission schools. Missions also pioneered female education — from girls’ schools in Tirunelveli and Bengal to Isabella Thoburn College, Lucknow (1886), the Women’s Christian College, Madras (1915), and the medical colleges at Ludhiana (1894) and Vellore (1900/1918) — and schooling for Dalit and Adivasi children excluded from village schools.

Print was the second great channel. Mission presses at Tranquebar, Serampore, Kottayam, Mangalore, Madras and Bombay cast Indian-script types, and Serampore published Samachar Darpan (1818), one of the first Bengali newspapers. Missionaries and Indian Christians compiled grammars and dictionaries, collected folklore and published textbooks, and Robert Caldwell’s Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian Languages (1856), by arguing for the independence of the Dravidian languages from Sanskrit, later fed the Tamil Dravidian movement.

On social reform, missionaries joined and sometimes led campaigns against sati (Carey and Ward gathered statistics; it was outlawed by Bentinck in 1829 with Rammohun Roy as the leading Indian voice), female infanticide, the pilgrim tax at Puri, hook-swinging and the dedication of girls as devadasis, and supported widow remarriage and the Age of Consent Act (1891). Their schools and churches offered Dalits education and new dignity, and Christian Nadar women’s struggle for the right to cover their breasts in Travancore (1813–59) and Christian participation in temple-road agitations such as Vaikom (1924–25) became part of wider movements against caste disability. Famine relief in 1876–78 and 1896–1900 brought orphanages and mass accessions, but also the charge that conversions were bought with food.

Indian responses were complex. Rammohun Roy admired the ethics of Jesus (The Precepts of Jesus, 1820) but rejected Trinitarian doctrine and debated Joshua Marshman; his Brahmo Samaj (1828) and Keshub Chunder Sen’s later movement absorbed Christian influences. Dayananda Saraswati’s Arya Samaj (1875) answered conversions with shuddhi reconversion, and Vivekananda presented a revitalised Hinduism to the West. Gandhi drew deeply on the Sermon on the Mount and befriended missionaries such as C. F. Andrews and E. Stanley Jones, yet opposed proselytisation, writing in 1935 that if he had the power to legislate he would stop it. B. R. Ambedkar seriously considered Christianity but in 1956 led his followers into Buddhism, citing caste divisions within the churches and Indian Christians’ political passivity.

After independence the debate entered the constitution and the courts. In the Constituent Assembly, Christian members accepted the end of separate electorates in return for guarantees of minority rights; Article 25 protected the freedom to “profess, practise and propagate” religion and Article 30 the right of minorities to run educational institutions. In 1956 the Niyogi Committee in Madhya Pradesh accused missions of using schools, hospitals and foreign money to convert the poor and recommended legal curbs; its report shaped the Odisha (1967) and Madhya Pradesh (1968) freedom-of-religion acts, which the Supreme Court upheld in Rev. Stainislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1977), holding that the right to propagate does not include a right to convert. In St Stephen’s College v. University of Delhi (1992) the court allowed Christian colleges to reserve a share of places for Christian students.

Historians remain divided over how to weigh this record. Older missionary histories celebrated civilising achievements; Hindu nationalist writers such as Sita Ram Goel and Arun Shourie (Missionaries in India, 1994) portrayed missions as an arm of imperialism and cultural aggression; and recent scholars — Robert Frykenberg, Susan Bayly, Geoffrey Oddie, Rupa Viswanath and others — emphasise Indian agency, the ways missionaries both challenged and accommodated caste, and their entanglement with colonial and landlord power. Census figures show that Christians today have markedly higher literacy (84.5 per cent in 2011 against 73.0 per cent nationally) and a more favourable sex ratio (1,023 women per 1,000 men against 943), though how far these reflect mission education rather than regional factors such as Kerala and the Northeast is debated.

indiaMissions.title: Caste in the churches, anti-conversion laws, violence and Dalit Christian rights
indiaMissions.region: All India, especially Odisha (Kandhamal, Keonjhar), Gujarat (Dangs), Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Manipur
indiaMissions.summary: Christians have remained about 2.3 per cent of India’s population in every census since 1951, yet questions of caste, conversion and minority rights have made them a focus of conflict: Dalit Christians are excluded from Scheduled Caste reservations under the 1950 presidential order, a growing number of states criminalise conversion by “force, fraud or allurement”, and episodes of violence — the killing of Graham Staines and his sons (1999), Kandhamal (2008), Manipur (2023) — coexist with internal caste discrimination within the churches themselves.
indiaMissions.story:
Caste is the oldest and most intimate tension. Most Indian Christians are of Dalit origin — estimates commonly range from half to two-thirds — but in many dioceses and parishes, especially in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala, caste survives inside the church: separate seating or entrances, separate cemeteries and festival processions, caste-based endogamy and the under-representation of Dalits among bishops and clergy. Clashes such as those at Eraiyur in Tamil Nadu in 2008 drew national attention, and Dalit Christian movements and the Dalit theology of Arvind P. Nirmal and others since the 1980s have demanded change. In 2016 the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of India issued a Policy of Dalit Empowerment acknowledging that untouchability and caste discrimination persist within the church.

The second tension concerns reservation. The Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order of 1950 restricted Scheduled Caste status to Hindus; Sikhs were added in 1956 and Buddhists in 1990, but Dalits who become Christians or Muslims lose access to reserved places in education, government jobs and legislatures, and to protection under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, though several states classify them as Other Backward Classes. Petitions seeking equal treatment have been pending before the Supreme Court since 2004. The Ranganath Misra Commission (2007) recommended delinking Scheduled Caste status from religion, but the central government did not accept its report, and in October 2022 it appointed a new commission under former Chief Justice K. G. Balakrishnan to examine the question; its report was reported to be complete in 2026 but had not been made public. Supporters argue that discrimination follows Dalits into the church; opponents, including some Hindu Dalit organisations, argue that untouchability is rooted in Hinduism and fear that extension would dilute existing quotas and encourage conversion. Because declaring oneself Christian can mean losing benefits, many scholars believe the census undercounts Christians, though the scale of this is disputed.

Third are the anti-conversion or “freedom of religion” laws. Odisha (1967) and Madhya Pradesh (1968) followed the Niyogi report, and the Supreme Court upheld them in Rev. Stainislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1977), ruling that the constitutional right to propagate religion does not include a right to convert another person. Arunachal Pradesh (1978), Gujarat (2003), Himachal Pradesh (2006, re-enacted 2019), Chhattisgarh (amending the inherited Madhya Pradesh law), Jharkhand (2017), Uttarakhand (2018), Uttar Pradesh (2020 ordinance, 2021 act, toughened in 2024), Madhya Pradesh (2021), Karnataka (2022), Haryana (2022) and Rajasthan (2025, with penalties up to life imprisonment) followed; Tamil Nadu passed such a law in 2002 but repealed it within a few years, and Karnataka’s Congress government decided in 2023 to repeal its act but had not completed repeal through the legislature. The laws typically penalise conversion by force, fraud, “allurement” or marriage, require prior notice to a district magistrate and, in newer versions, allow third-party complaints and shift the burden of proof to the accused. Their defenders say they protect poor and vulnerable people from predatory proselytism; critics, including civil-liberties groups, argue that their vague definitions criminalise ordinary charity and worship, that convictions are rare, and that they are used to justify police action and vigilante attacks on prayer meetings.

Violence against Christians became a national issue in 1998–99. Attacks on churches and Christian villages in the Dangs district of Gujarat around Christmas 1998 were followed, on the night of 22–23 January 1999, by the burning to death of the Australian missionary Graham Staines — who had worked among leprosy patients at Baripada in Mayurbhanj since 1965 — and his sons Philip (10) and Timothy (6) in their vehicle at Manoharpur in Keonjhar district, Odisha, by a mob led by Dara Singh, a man linked to Hindu militant activism. The Wadhwa Commission attributed the crime to Dara Singh and his associates; he was sentenced to death in 2003, commuted to life imprisonment by the Orissa High Court in 2005 and upheld by the Supreme Court in 2011. Gladys Staines publicly forgave the killers, continued the leprosy work and received the Padma Shri in 2005. Kandhamal in Odisha, where tensions between Kandha (Kui) Adivasis and Christian Panas (Dalits) over land and Scheduled Tribe status had been mobilised by Hindu nationalist groups, saw riots at Christmas 2007; after the murder of the Hindu leader Swami Lakshmanananda Saraswati on 23 August 2008 — claimed by Maoists, though seven Christians were later convicted in a trial widely criticised — weeks of violence followed. Official figures recorded 39 deaths, while church and civil-society sources estimate around 100; some 300–400 churches and places of worship and about 5,600–6,000 houses were destroyed and over 50,000 people displaced. In 2016 the Supreme Court ordered increased compensation and the re-examination of 315 cases in which police had failed to prosecute. Attacks on churches in and around Mangalore (2008) and the ethnic conflict in Manipur from May 2023 — fundamentally a struggle between the largely Hindu Meitei and largely Christian Kuki-Zo over land and tribal status, in which more than 250 people died, about 60,000 were displaced and hundreds of churches, including Meitei churches, were burned — added to the record.

In the 2010s and 2020s pressure took broader forms. The United Christian Forum’s helpline recorded 734 incidents of violence and harassment against Christians in 2023 and 834 in 2024, most commonly following accusations of forced conversion, with Uttar Pradesh and Chhattisgarh the worst affected; the government disputes such counts. Amendments to the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act in 2010 and 2020 led to the cancellation of thousands of NGO licences, including Christian charities; Compassion International ended its Indian programmes in 2017, and the Missionaries of Charity’s licence was briefly refused renewal in 2021. “Ghar wapsi” reconversion campaigns and demands, revived in the 2020s, to delist Christian and Muslim converts from Scheduled Tribe status — an idea first proposed by the Congress MP Kartik Oraon around 1967–70 — target tribal Christians. The United States Commission on International Religious Freedom has recommended since 2020 that India be designated a Country of Particular Concern; the Indian government rejects its reports as biased.

The picture is not uniform. In Kerala, Goa and the Christian-majority states of Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya, Christians are fully part of public life and some Christian groups have aligned with the BJP; in Kerala tension has also arisen between some Catholic leaders and Muslims, as in the controversy over a bishop’s “narcotic jihad” remarks in 2021. A Pew Research Center survey (2021) found that most Indian Christians, like most Hindus, value religious tolerance while preferring to live and marry within their own community. Scholars such as Chad Bauman link anti-Christian violence to local competition over conversion — particularly with fast-growing Pentecostal churches — to tribal and Dalit status politics, and to Hindu nationalist mobilisation, while Hindu nationalist writers frame the issue as defence of indigenous culture against foreign-funded proselytism.
